items.title: Online Taalhuis: kansen, uitdagingen en praktijk
items.raw_text: Online taalactiviteiten maken taalondersteuning toegankelijker voor mensen die niet altijd naar de bibliotheek kunnen komen of overdag niet beschikbaar zijn. Steeds meer bibliotheken breiden hun fysieke a anbod uit met online taalactiviteiten . We organiseerden een Summerschool over dit onderwerp, en daarom verzamelde ik praktische inzichten hierover. Ik ging in gesprek met Paula Sangers, senior medewerker Basisvaardigheden en coördinator van een online Taalcafé van Bibliotheek Zuid-Hollandse Eilanden. In dit artikel lees je de kansen, uitdagingen en aandachtspunten van online taalactiviteiten . Voordelen van online taalactiviteit en Een online aanbod maakt het mogelijk om doelgroepen te bereiken die anders moeilijk deelnemen aan activiteiten van het Taalhuis. Daarbij kan je denken aan bv. intakegesprek, Taalcafe,taalcoaching, leesclub, ezv. Voor mensen die overdag werken, ouders met jonge kinderen of inwoners die verder van de bibliotheek wonen, biedt een online Taalhuis vaak de flexibiliteit die nodig is om toch mee te doen. Ook voor mantelzorgers, mensen met gezondheidsproblemen of een beperkte mobiliteit kan online deelname een uitkomst zijn. Een ander voordeel is dat zowel deelnemers als begeleiders kunnen aansluiten vanuit huis, onderweg of vanaf een andere locatie. Op deze manier kunnen de taalleerders in contact met de taal blijven ook vanuit buitenland. De deelname wordt minder afhankelijk van reistijd, vakanties en bereikbaarheid. items.title: Dit organiseerden bibliotheken tijdens Wereld Alzheimer Dag

items.title: Visietraject bij MFCO Rozet: de kunst van impactgericht werken
items.raw_text: Ga je een verandertraject altijd in omdat iets niet goed gaat? Nee, blijkt uit het verhaal van Rozet. Bij deze Arnhemse multifunctionele culturele organisatie (MFCO) zaten de adviseurs Taal en Cultuur behoorlijk op een lijn. De samenwerking binnen team Educatie verliep organisch en intuïtief. Toch was er behoefte aan ondersteuning bij een gezamenlijke visie. Ook wilde het team antwoord op de vraag ‘doen we de juiste dingen en hebben die de juiste impact?’ Daar kwam Rijnbrink in beeld. Voor meer samenhang, structuur en expertise in de kunst van impactgericht werken. In dit artikel lees je de ervaringen van Roos de Ridder en Nataschenka le Clercq van Rozet en onze eigen adviseur Evelien Wietsma. Hoe pakten ze het visietraject aan? Wat leverde het op? En welke adviezen hebben ze voor andere bibliotheken en MFCO’s? De kracht van verbinding Nataschenka en Roos zijn sinds kort teamleider van team Educatie bij Rozet. Daarnaast hebben ze andere functies en taken: van projectleider Cultuureducatie met Kwaliteit tot projectleider de Bibliotheek op school en leesconsulent. Die diversiteit is illustratief voor de manier van werken en de visie van Rozet. ‘Als adviseurs gaan we met basisscholen in gesprek over de hele breedte van taal, kunst en erfgoed’, vertelt Nataschenka. ‘Vanuit hun behoeften organiseren we verschillende projecten en samenwerkingen. items.title: Schuren mag! 7x inzichten over democratie en burgerschap
items.raw_text: Een literaire avond in je bibliotheek over een onderwerp dat gevoelig ligt. Een school die een collectie afwijst vanwege levensovertuigingen. Of een gesprek tussen mensen die lijnrecht tegenover elkaar staan… Als bibliotheek ben je er voor iedereen. Maar kun je er eigenlijk wel voor iedereen zijn? En hoe ga je om met meningen die botsen met elkaar, of misschien zelfs met die van jou? Op 24 september gingen zo’n 350 bibliotheekprofessionals hierover met elkaar in gesprek tijdens het Kennisfestival Democratie & Burgerschap , georganiseerd door SPN . In dit artikel delen we de belangrijkste inzichten van de dag. Als bibliotheek heb je een belangrijke rol in het versterken van democratie en burgerschap. Die opdracht staat ook beschreven in het Bibliotheekconvenant 2024-2027 . Democratie is niet vanzelfsprekend. Het vraagt om aandacht, oefening en soms ook moed. Willeke Slingerland is lector Sociale Cohesie en de Democratische Rechtsstaat aan de Hogeschool Utrecht. Zij kreeg het publiek tijdens de dagopening muisstil met haar verhaal over de rol van de bibliotheek in het beschermen van de democratie. Zij stelt: ‘Bibliotheken zijn de kanaries, oftewel waakhonden, van de democratie. items.title: AI-vermeldingen, CAPTCHA en meer: praktische tips voor privacy en informatiebeveiliging
items.raw_text: Privacy en informatiebeveiliging blijven actuele onderwerpen voor bibliotheken. Sinds 2 augustus is het bijvoorbeeld verplicht om transparant te zijn over gebruik van AI. Om jullie zo goed mogelijk op de hoogte te houden, delen we iedere twee maanden het laatste nieuws, ontwikkelingen, praktische tips en opleidingsmogelijkheden op het gebied van privacy en informatiebeveiliging. items.title: Maak kennis met Constance: de kracht achter de onderwijscollecties
items.raw_text: Tussen de boekenkasten in het collectiegebouw van Rijnbrink werkt Constance Melissen. Als collectiebeheerder Onderwijs zorgt zij ervoor dat scholen boeken krijgen die aansluiten bij hun lessen én de leefwereld van kinderen en jongeren. Zo draagt ze bij aan leesplezier bij de jeugd. In dit artikel maak je kennis met Constance en het werk dat zij doet. Wie regelmatig op een basisschool komt, herkent het meteen: de themahoek. Vaak vol met boeken in een bepaald thema. Soms door de leerkracht aangevuld met accessoires. Een thema is bijvoorbeeld kerst, of vervoer. Maar ook duurzaamheid of sprookjes. Bij Rijnbrink noemen we dit onderwijscollecties. De boeken zijn verzameld rondom een thema. Ze sluiten aan bij de leefwereld van kinderen en passen bij het niveau van verschillende leeftijdsgroepen in het basisonderwijs en de kinderopvang. Zo ontdekken kinderen nieuwe onderwerpen en lezen ze boeken die aansluiten bij hun interesses en ontwikkeling. Ook helpt het de leraren bij het geven van hun lessen. Scholen kunnen zelf online een themacollectie bestellen en deze zes weken lenen. Werken tussen de boeken Constance is verantwoordelijk voor de onderwijscollecties. Zij bepaalt welke boeken bij een thema passen. En zorgt ervoor dat het pakket met themaboeken bij de scholen komen. Haar werk doet ze letterlijk tussen de boeken. items.title: Frisse financiële start in 2027? 5x tips voor jouw jaarafsluiting
items.raw_text: Het jaar loopt op zijn einde. Een mooi moment om even stil te staan, terug te kijken en vooruit te denken. Wat ging er goed, wat kan beter? Wat moet er financieel nog geregeld worden? En welke kansen liggen er voor het nieuwe jaar? Een zorgvuldige jaarafsluiting geeft je rust, overzicht en een vliegende start voor 2026. Met deze 5 praktische tips maak je de jaarovergang soepel en benut je alle kansen die het nieuwe jaar biedt. items.title: Op weg naar slimmer en duurzamer transport
items.raw_text: We merken het allemaal aan de pomp: de prijs van brandstof is hoog. Maandelijks betaalt Rijnbrink nu €3.000 meer aan brandstof dan een jaar geleden. Het is daarom noodzakelijk om efficiënt en duurzaam te rijden. Misschien merk je dat als bibliotheek of school, omdat we materialen op een andere tijd bezorgen dan je gewend bent. In dit artikel vertellen collega’s Hans Bender en Daan Meijer van Facilitair & Logistiek over hoe zij werken aan efficiënt en toekomstbestendig transport. Waar willen zij naartoe? Welke uitdagingen zijn er? En wat betekent dit voor jullie? Hans en Daan kijken vanaf hun werkruimte uit op het wagenpark van Rijnbrink. Vanuit de distributiehal vertrekken dagelijks bestel- en vrachtauto’s naar scholen en bibliotheken in Gelderland en Overijssel. Wekelijks bezoeken onze chauffeurs zo’n 210 vestigingen en maken zij ongeveer 650 stops. Niet alle voertuigen gaan iedere dag de weg op. Hans: ‘Van de elf wagens die eerst dagelijks reden, rijden er nu nog maar negen. Zo rijden we efficiënter en duurzamer.’ Minder routes, andere tijden Om dit mogelijk te maken, pasten we afgelopen zomer enkele routes aan. Door bestaande routes uit te breiden, konden we vijf routes per week schrappen. Dat bespaart brandstof en vermindert de uitstoot. Voor sommige bibliotheken betekent dit dat de chauffeur op een ander tijdstip langskomt dan voorheen. items.title: Groeien in je rol als vrijwilligerscoördinator, hoe doe je dat?
items.raw_text: Voor iedere beroepskracht werken er bij openbare bibliotheken gemiddeld ruim drie vrijwilligers. Samen houden zij de bibliotheek draaiend. Goede samenwerking en begeleiding zijn dus belangrijk; onderwerpen waar vrijwilligerscoördinatoren volop mee bezig zijn. Hun rol verandert. items.title: Prinsjesdag 2026: 5 thema’s uitgelicht voor bibliotheken
items.raw_text: Prinsjesdag 2026 zit erop. De nieuw gepresenteerde plannen laten zien dat het kabinet vertrouwen heeft in de toekomst van bibliotheken. Er komt meer zekerheid voor leesbevordering, bibliotheken krijgen een belangrijke maatschappelijke rol en er is geld voor verdere ontwikkeling. Tegelijkertijd zijn er ook uitdagingen. items.title: Lezen dichter bij studenten: de kracht van samenwerken
items.raw_text: Zeven schoolbibliotheken op zeven locaties. Dat is het doel van de samenwerking tussen ROC van Twente, vier Overijsselse bibliotheken en Rijnbrink. Een mooi voorbeeld van hoe bovenlokale samenwerking lezen dichter bij studenten kan brengen. En van hoe we ze samen veel meer bijbrengen dan een vak. Erwin Karst was als adviseur bij Rijnbrink aanjager van deze bovenlokale samenwerking. items.title: Vacature directeur / bestuurder
items.raw_text: Wil jij richting geven aan een organisatie die overheid, bedrijfsleven, kenniswereld en maatschappij bij elkaar brengt op het gebied van digitalisering? items.title: Nederlanders denken dat ze phishing herkennen, maar AI maakt oplichting steeds echter en juist dát is een groot veiligheidsrisico
items.raw_text: Uit het jaarlijkse nationale cybersecurityonderzoek van Alert Online, mede mogelijk gemaakt door het ministerie van Economische Zaken en Klimaat, blijkt dat Nederlanders wél weten wat veilig online gedrag is, maar gemiddeld slechts een derde van de veilige handelingen consequent toepassen. Den Haag – Nederlanders weten goed hoe ze zich online moeten beschermen, maar vertrouwen opvallend vaak op hun eigen vermogen om gevaar te herkennen. Zodra er meer van hen gevraagd wordt dan kijken, neemt de motivatie om zich veilig te gedragen af. Slechts één op de zes gebruikt altijd tweefactorauthenticatie, een dubbel slot voor je accounts en apparaten dat ervoor zorgt dat er meer nodig is dan een wachtwoord om in te loggen. Zo kunnen criminelen met een gestolen wachtwoord niet zomaar een account overnemen. En maar drie op de tien gaan altijd zelf naar de officiële website in plaats van op een link te klikken. Dat blijkt uit het nationale cybersecurityonderzoek van Alert Online, dat vandaag verschijnt bij de start van de Europese cybersecuritymaand. Wie denkt zelf phishing te herkennen, slaat in veel gevallen de stappen over die je écht beschermen. items.title: Van regisserende naar ontwerpende overheid
items.raw_text: Van AI-experiment naar digitaal opdrachtgeverschap Veranderverhalen vanuit ECP | Platform voor de Informatiesamenleving ECP | Platform voor de Informatiesamenleving brengt met een reeks veranderverhalen in beeld hoe professionals binnen de overheid werken aan betekenisvolle digitalisering. In de gesprekken met Marc Minnee en Marco de Bruijn van het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties (BZK) staat centraal waar verandering daadwerkelijk ontstaat: wanneer professionals elkaar vinden, aannames bespreekbaar maken en keuzes maken die bijdragen aan versnelling én duurzame borging. Zo laten de verhalen zien hoe digitalisering door concrete interventies kan bijdragen aan een toekomstgerichte overheid waarin burgers en ondernemers centraal staan, met blijvende aandacht voor ethiek, privacy, security en maatschappelijk vertrouwen. Op 24 juni vond in Amare voor de vijfde keer de CIO-dag plaats. Voor een zaal vol CIO’s schetsten Marc Minnee, innovatiemanager voor het ministerie van BZK, en Marco de Bruijn, beleidsmedewerker AI bij het ministerie van BZK, hun NDS AI-visie op de inzet van generatieve AI-modellen bij de overheid. Hun verhaal begint bij taalmodellen, maar raakt al snel aan een veel fundamentelere vraag: hoe houdt de overheid zelf regie over haar digitale toekomst? items.title: OTC Whitepaper Soevereiniteit
items.raw_text: Digitale soevereiniteit betekent niet dat organisaties alle digitale diensten zelf moeten bezitten of beheren. Het betekent dat zij aantoonbare grip hebben op kritieke digitale afhankelijkheden: inzicht in de keten, bewuste risicoacceptatie, uitvoerbare alternatieven, onafhankelijke controle en transparante communicatie over keuzes en restrisico’s. In het whitepaper over digitale soevereiniteit vertaalt de Online Trust Coalitie dit thema naar een praktisch handelingskader voor bestuurders, IT-verantwoordelijken, toezichthouders, serviceproviders en risk- en compliancefuncties. De OTC stelt dat digitale soevereiniteit niet draait om volledige autonomie of autarkie, maar om aantoonbare beheersing: inzicht in kritieke digitale afhankelijkheden, expliciete risicoafweging, uitvoerbare exit-mogelijkheden, onafhankelijke controle en heldere communicatie over restrisico’s en gemaakte keuzes. De OTC signaleert dat impliciet vertrouwen in digitale diensten onder druk staat. Geopolitieke spanningen, conflicterende rechtsstelsels, concentratie van leveranciersmacht en complexe beheerketens maken zichtbaar dat organisaties niet langer kunnen volstaan met contracten, certificaten of algemene toezeggingen. items.title: ‘Veranderen doe je via consensus én met fermheid’
items.raw_text: Binnen Digitaal Doordacht onderzoeken we hoe digitalisering in de publieke sector daadwerkelijk bijdraagt aan betere dienstverlening, meer openheid en groter vertrouwen. Het veranderverhaal van Jolein Baidenmann laat zien dat echte openheid niet draait om simpelweg méér informatie openbaar maken, maar om informatie die voor mensen daadwerkelijk begrijpelijk en bruikbaar is. Wat haar aanpak bijzonder maakt, is hoe zij in een complexe publieke omgeving beweging creëert: door belangen zichtbaar te maken, partijen te verbinden en draagvlak te combineren met duidelijke keuzes. “Soms moet je als leider keuzes maken en stevig zijn: ik heb iedereen gehoord, maar we gaan toch die kant op.” Jolein Baidenmann is verandermanager en werkt met die insteek aan een overheid die openheid op een betekenisvolle manier probeert waar te maken. “Het is belangrijk dat een open overheid de samenleving in staat stelt om mee te denken, te controleren en gebruik te maken van de informatie die bij de overheid beschikbaar is.” Als manager Open Overheid en plaatsvervangend directeur Open Overheid bij het ministerie van Binnenlandse Zaken en Koninkrijksrelaties (BZK) is Baidenmann bij uitstek de persoon om het concept ‘open overheid’ in praktijk te brengen. items.title: Australian Public Libraries Statistical Report 2024–25
items.raw_text: Australians are using their public libraries in growing numbers, with visits, borrowing and participation in library programs continuing to rise despite increasing pressure on funding and staffing. The Australian Public Libraries Statistical Report 2024–25 , released by the Australian Library and Information Association (ALIA) and National and State Libraries Australasia (NSLA), provides a national snapshot of public library services and how Australians are using them. The figures tell a good news story, with Australian communities increasingly turning to their public libraries for collections, spaces, online services, programs and activities. Physical and online library visits increased by 8.5% in a single year, reaching a five-year high of more than 160 million visits. Public library collections were used almost 180 million times, while a record 434,000 library programs attracted more than 7.2 million attendees. Digital engagement also continues to grow, with digital collection use increasing by 80% over five years and Wi-Fi use almost doubling since 2021–22. Libraries are increasingly being used as places to meet, work and connect, with meeting-room use up 24% in the past year and 81% since 2021–22. Despite the steady increase in usage, public libraries are meeting this heightened demand within an increasingly constrained funding environment. items.title: IFLA turns 99: The countdown begins!
items.raw_text: Today IFLA celebrates its 99th birthday. Some might say that only big, round number anniversaries should be celebrated, but we haven’t made it this far by following the crowd. So, let us be defiant of expectations, and make today also an opportunity to celebrate, looking back to what we have achieved, but also looking forward to what awaits us in 2027 and well beyond. What is IFLA now, almost a century after its creation? A global community made of over 1600 members and more than 1000 active, passionate volunteers working hard to change the library field for the better. A place where we celebrate the past but look at technology, knowledge and innovation with optimism in order to achieve sustainable futures for all. An organisation that has always striven to make the world a better place. Libraries make our lives better and IFLA supports libraries globally through its international advocacy, professional standards, capacity building, and resource sharing. We have got this far because our core mission and values are lasting, giving us a key reference point and source of resilience in times of change. Today, like so many times in the past, we and the societies are being shaped and reshaped by dramatic political, economic, environmental, and social trends. items.title: Authors Discuss Being Banned, Part 2: Malinda Lo, Ellen Hopkins, and Jennifer L. Armentrout
items.raw_text: The troubling trend of book challenges and bans in libraries across the US continues. In 2025, 4,235 titles were banned or challenged at public, school, or university libraries, according to the American Library Association’s (ALA) State of America’s Libraries 2026 report. This figure was the second highest (following the record set in 2023) since ALA’s Office for Intellectual Freedom (OIF) began documenting censorship attempts in 1990. Behind each title is an author being professionally—and sometimes personally—targeted for the stories they have chosen to share. These works usually amplify marginalized voices such as abuse victims or those within the LGBTQ+ community. American Libraries spoke with five authors on the Top 11 Most Challenged Books of 2025 list included in the report to hear how their experiences affected them. Interviews have been edited for space and clarity. Read Part 1 for the first two interviews with Patricia McCormick and Stephen Chbosky. Set in 1950s San Francisco, the book tells the story of 17-year-old Lily Hu as she navigates falling in love in a place and time not ready to accept a same-sex couple. items.title: Refreshing for the Future
items.raw_text: Library renovations can feel overwhelming—especially when you’re juggling tight budgets, big community expectations, and a building that’s showing its age. The good news is you don’t have to choose between “do nothing” and “tear it down.” Most successful library upgrades live somewhere in the middle: a smart, phased plan that protects your long-term vision while making meaningful improvements right now. Here are a few practical ways to think about approaching a library renovation: Start with a North Star. Before you pick finishes or start talking timelines, take a step back and get clarity on what you want your library to become. I call this the north star —your vision for how the building should function for staff and the public. Even if you only have funding for part of the work today, guiding principles help you avoid spending money on changes you’ll undo later. Renovations are much easier when everyone can point to the same end goal—even if you’re getting there in phases. Assess the building first. It’s tempting to jump straight into visible improvements, but understanding existing conditions is what sets a project up for success. A solid facility-condition evaluation looks at the status of major building systems and flags components that may be nearing the end of their life cycle, such as mechanical systems, electrical panel capacity, and even finishes like carpet. items.title: Limiting Risk in the Face of Uncertainty
items.raw_text: If you save for retirement when you are young, the standard advice is to emphasize stock-based exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds. Stocks increase and decrease in dramatic ways that no one can predict reliably, so this approach carries some risk. Fortunately for US stock market investors, that risk has historically been rewarded, on average and over the long term, with high returns. As you approach retirement and need to rely on investments to cover living expenses, the standard advice is to shift your portfolio toward bond-based ETFs or mutual funds. Bonds have had fewer and less dramatic booms and busts. For this reason, they are generally considered less risky than stocks. On average, over the long term, bonds’ safety has meant lower, more reliable returns than stocks. Risk makes less sense for ALA right now. Because of its financial deficit , the Association needs stability. Therefore, in April, ALA’s Endowment Trustees updated the target allocation for the Association’s investment portfolio, reducing our holdings of stocks from 50% to 40%, and increasing ALA’s holdings of bonds from 30% to 40%. As a result, we are sacrificing some projected returns to limit projected risk. If stocks boom as they have in the past few years, ALA’s portfolio will not increase as much as it would have. More than two-thirds of this year’s 15 selections are renovations or adaptive reuse projects. Libraries of all types are finding ways to acknowledge historical and environmental realities, embrace natural elements and cultural identities, evolve traditions, and build in flexibility to account for the unexpected. Read on for snapshots of these communities in motion. Natural immersion Maplewood (N.J.) Memorial Library Adjacent to a historic park, with protected natural areas on all sides, this 1955 masonry structure had nowhere to expand but up. The new, light-filled second floor features bird-safe glass, wood battens, and green roofs for a treehouse feel. The all-electric building, the first LEED Gold–certified library in New Jersey, includes solar panels that offset more than half of the library’s energy use. items.title: Secrets of Effective Upskilling
items.raw_text: This is an excerpt from Upskilling for Library Workers: A Guide for Future-Ready Professionals by Ann Medaille (ALA Editions, 2026). With the advent of new technologies and rapid social and economic shifts, library workers’ jobs are being transformed. Compared with a decade ago, library workers now spend more time consulting on complex research tools, teaching digital literacy classes, supporting virtual learning environments, helping users troubleshoot devices, and codesigning projects with community partners. The pace at which library staffers are called upon to learn new skills is accelerating, and workers may struggle to keep up. In addition, automation and artificial intelligence (AI) are altering many aspects of work. In the long run, technological innovations have the potential to increase productivity and lead to more interesting kinds of work, but in the short term, they often cause disruptions that can be difficult for workers to navigate. To address these changes—and manage the anxieties that come along with them—workers need constant support for skill development. While corporations may embrace upskilling to stay competitive, libraries will have to support upskilling to remain relevant. Library leaders are under greater pressure to respond rapidly to changing social and economic conditions and demonstrate that their libraries make a difference in their communities. items.title: Hold the Phone
items.raw_text: Since fall 2024, each school day at Grant High School in Portland, Oregon, has started the same way: Roughly 2,100 students line up to place their phones in gray and green Yondr pouches—the kind live performers use to prevent audience members from recording—as they enter the building. From the morning bell to dismissal, phones are sealed and can be unlocked only with special magnets near the school’s exits as students leave for the day. The high school’s effort to limit phone use on campus has received support from its educators, who say classroom engagement is on the rise, and mixed reviews from students, who dislike being cut off from their devices. But there’s been one unexpected outcome of the policy: More students are spending time in the library, where they’re browsing the collection or hanging out during free periods, says teacher-librarian Paige Battle. “They’re checking out more books, and I feel like that’s been so important in their education,” Battle says. “We’re seeing studies about students, even adults, not having the reading stamina they’ve had in the past, so I’ve been encouraged by this increase.” Roughly six in 10 parents of an 11- or 12-year-old say their child owns a smartphone, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center survey . items.raw_text: From PEN America: PEN America today reported nearly 12,000 book bans in public schools nationwide during the 2025-2026 school year—the largest number in a single year. New state censorship laws accounted for much of the increase, coupled with the use of artificial intelligence to remove books en masse including popular manga series and other graphic novels. In a report released to coincide with Banned Books Week, the latest accounting of book bans increased to 34,000 instances since PEN America began documenting the spreading book censorship crisis in schools in 2021. Texas recorded the largest number of book bans during the 2025-2026 school year (over 8,100), surpassing Florida (over 3,200), due to the impact of a censorial Texas law, SB13, which bans broad categories of books in schools. Florida had been No. 1 for three consecutive years. Most Banned Titles and Authors (PEN America 2026) The writers and free expression organization also reported a record number of unique titles banned in the last school year—more than 7,000—which impacted more than 4,000 authors, illustrators and translators, also a record number. In addition, researchers identified 114 school districts that had banned books over the year, the highest number ever for a single year according to PEN America ’s Index of School Book Bans. items.title: Elena, Aris, Marcus: : AI-Generated ‘Ghosts’ are Polluting the Scientific Literature
items.raw_text: From Nature: Elena Vasquez spent three months camping on the rim of Mount Nyiragongo in the Democratic Republic of the Congo back in 2019. She says the sulfur dioxide there smelt like “burnt matches mixed with rotten eggs”. Her colleague, Marcus Chen, has witnessed 11 volcanic eruptions across four continents. Vasquez and Chen’s accounts appeared on Volcanoes Explored, a now-defunct website that described itself as a resource for “exploring the dynamic world of volcanoes”. But there’s a problem: these tales are not real and the pair of volcanology specialists is made up. Vasquez and Chen are ‘ghost’ identities generated by Claude — the large language model (LLM) made by Anthropic in San Francisco — when prompted by users to create fictional experts, according to a preprint published in June. Gemini, Google’s LLM, was found to use a different pair of recurring characters, called Aris Thorne and Lena Petrova, and OpenAI’s GPT repeatedly used the name Elara Voss. [Clip] Fake experts such as these can be found across the Internet as everything from blockchain specialists and astronauts to board members and podcast hosts, and they raise specific concerns around integrity of the scientific literature, say Neo Christopher Chung and Michał Brzozowski, computer scientists at the Samsung AI Center Warsaw in Poland and co-authors of the preprint. items.title: Mellon Foundation Releases: “Mapping the Landscape of Community-Based Archives” Report
items.raw_text: From the Mellon Foundation: Today, the Mellon Foundation released “Powerful but Precarious: Mapping the Landscape of Community-Based Archives,” the first national study of its kind. Produced in partnership with research firm Engage R+D, the study draws on a survey of 336 independent, community-led archives, and in-depth interviews with more than 20 practitioners across the country. Community-based archives are independent organizations that collect and preserve the records, photographs, oral histories, personal papers, and other artifacts of communities many of which have been historically excluded from mainstream institutions. Unlike institutional archives, community-based archives often hold materials that exist nowhere else – collections that, if lost, cannot be recovered. Additionally, community-based archives often operate outside of the context of universities, libraries, historical societies, or other collecting institutions and in doing so, they serve as civic infrastructure where people can access and learn about their own localized or underexplored histories. While hundreds of these archives exist across the United States, serving communities of every background and geography, they have never been mapped, counted, or examined at this scale—leaving them largely invisible to the funders, policymakers, and organizations best positioned to support them. items.title: Report: Chinese-Owned Science Journal Created to Rival the Best
items.raw_text: From Nature: A new Chinese-owned journal has set its sights on rivalling the world’s oldest and most influential academic titles. Vita is one of several English-language journals that have launched in China in the past couple of years. They represent the country’s latest effort to create prestigious global journals, as part of the government’s Journal Excellence Action Plan, which began in 2019. [Clip] Vita is jointly funded by the Higher Education Press, a subsidiary of China’s Ministry of Education based in Beijing, and Westlake University in Hangzhou, its editorial team says. It publishes papers in biological sciences. Its first print issue came out in July. As an open-access journal, Vita waives article-processing charges (APCs), fees many publishers require authors to pay when publishing open access articles. [Clip] Vita ’s model is “clearly going to be appealing” to authors, says James Butcher, a former publisher who runs a consultancy firm called Journalology near Liverpool, UK. But he warns that keeping the model running in the long term will be a challenge for the journal and its funders because “publishing is expensive”. Publishers who charge APCs say that the money helps to cover the costs of publishing open access, including paying the salaries of in-house editors and production staff, as well as printing and server costs. Drawing on 771 responses, this year’s report provides an opportunity to look beyond a single snapshot and begin tracking how AI adoption, attitudes, policies, and concerns are changing over time. [Clip] An Industry Moving Toward More Structured AI Use One of the clearest changes from 2025 is happening at the organizational level. In 2026, 63% of respondents said their organization is using AI, up from 48% in 2025. Individual use moved in the opposite direction, falling from 46% to 38%. Organization size also matters: 88% of organizations with more than 100 employees reported using AI. Adoption does not necessarily mean unrestricted use. The most common organizational approach is to encourage AI within controlled workflows or for specific tasks, while 49% of respondents said their organization now has an official AI policy or guidelines, up from 31% in 2025. items.title: Report: Oxford Lets OpenAI Train Its AI Models On Historical Texts From the Bodleian Library
items.raw_text: From The Guardian: The University of Oxford has allowed the company behind ChatGPT to train its AI models on historical texts from its Bodleian Library, as tech companies scour academic institutions for fresh data. The Bodleian material digitised by OpenAI has been used to “populate the OpenAI training set”, according to internal documents. Oxford announced a partnership with the company in March 2025, using OpenAI software to digitise texts from the university’s world-famous library, which it said would make the content more widely available for students and researchers. However, the announcement did not state the material would be used for training OpenAI’s models, which are trained to recognise patterns in words – and thus “learn” to write complete sentences and perform other cognitive tasks – by being fed vast amounts of data. [Clip] Meeting minutes at the University of Oxford, obtained via a freedom of information request, record concerns from staff, including members of the Bodleian governance committee, about the reputational risk of partnering with OpenAI and the effect on the university’s environmental commitments of striking a deal involving an energy-intensive technology. The network is live and open to the public at okn.us . NSF OKN provides a structured, persistent, verifiable knowledge layer to complement contemporary artificial intelligence models, providing grounding of facts, attribution, and knowledge governance essential to critical AI applications in a number of fields. OKN’s value goes beyond machines querying structured knowledge: Its deeper value provides AI systems with a shared, explicit, interoperable, and auditable representation of the world on which they are expected to reason and act. Across science, government, and many key enterprise applications, valuable datasets sit in silos that are not accessible, interoperable, nor ready for use by AI systems. OKN makes federal and public data findable, connected, and machine-readable at a national scale. items.raw_text: After thirty years of keeping libraries online, the E-Rate program has seen its share of challenges. Just in the last two years, the program weathered the loss of support for hotspot lending and suffered through a Supreme Court Challenge . While the Supreme Court decision ultimately went in our favor, there is no time to sit back and relax for library advocates. In June, the Federal Communication’s Commission (FCC) launched a proceeding (officially, a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking) that threatens to terminate this vital program. Now is the time to show up for E-Rate and tell the FCC what broadband access at your library means for your community. A Quick E-Rate Refresher One of four programs within the FCC’s Universal Service Fund, set up in the 1996 Telecommunications Act, the E-Rate program was established to ensure public libraries and K-12 schools have affordable access to advanced telecommunications (i.e., broadband and internet access). Today, E-Rate provides funding to almost three-quarters of public libraries to help offset monthly internet service costs and the costs for eligible technology necessary for making sure Wi-Fi is available throughout the building. items.title: Art for Everyone: How Public Libraries Expand Access
items.raw_text: Introducing children to viewing, creating, and enjoying art at a young age helps them appreciate it throughout their lives. Some children are exposed to various forms of art because it is part of their daily life or because they have easy access to museums and galleries in their community. But in many areas across the country, access to museums and art galleries can be cost prohibitive. That is where the public library comes in! While some museums, including the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, D.C., offer free admission, millions of people across the country do not have easy access to them. According to the 2024 Annual Survey of Museum-Goers from the American Alliance of Museums and Wilkening Consulting, museum admission costs vary widely, from a few dollars to $40–$50 per adult at some institutions. Among U.S. adults who visit museums at least occasionally, cost was the number one barrier to visiting more often. Among frequent museum-goers, younger adults were twice as likely as seniors to be concerned about admission costs. In response to those barriers, and in an effort to enrich and inspire customers of all ages, many library systems have stepped up to provide access to art in a variety of forms. items.title: The Librarian’s New Role: Knowledge Discovery
items.raw_text: For more than thirty years I have been interested in one deceptively simple question: How do we find things? At first glance, the answer appears obvious. We search. But anyone who has spent a lifetime in libraries knows that searching and finding are not the same thing. Throughout my earlier articles in Public Libraries Online , I explored several aspects of this process. In Finding Answers , I argued that patrons rarely come looking for information; they come looking for answers. In Search vs. Research , I suggested that locating information is only the beginning of inquiry. In Keeping Things Found , I examined what happens after discovery, how knowledge is preserved, organized, and made retrievable for future use. Artificial intelligence is now transforming how people search and, perhaps more importantly, how they find. For the first time in history, millions of people no longer begin by opening a directory, consulting an index, or scanning pages of search results. Instead, they ask a question in ordinary language and receive what appears to be a finished answer. This is more than another improvement in search technology. It represents a fundamental change in the relationship between people and information. The question librarians should be asking is not whether artificial intelligence can answer questions. items.title: How Library Science Principles Power Community AI Literacy
items.raw_text: Public libraries are dealing with budget cuts, book bans, and the usual existential questions about whether anyone needs physical collections when they can google everything. And now AI shows up, and everyone assumes libraries are about to get steamrolled by it too. But watch what’s happening at reference desks across the country. Patrons ask how to determine whether an IRS email is real or a phishing attempt generated by AI. Small business owners are trying to figure out which AI tool won’t steal their marketing copy. Retired community members want to use AI to parse dense municipal documents but do not know where to start. A parent is concerned about their teenager using AI for homework and whether that’s cheating. These aren’t edge cases. This is what reference work looks like now. Much has been written about how libraries can use AI tools internally—chatbots for reference, algorithms for cataloging, and predictive analytics for collection development. But there’s another question we need to answer: How do libraries help communities navigate AI? And here’s what I realized while building AI governance frameworks: these are not computer science problems. They’re library science problems—questions about provenance, access, evaluation, and trust. The exact questions libraries have been answering for over a century, just dressed up in a new syntax. items.title: Tag! You’re It: RFID’s Big Play in Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Radio Frequency Identification (RFID) technology has become one of the most influential innovations shaping the future of library operations. Since its introduction into library settings in the late 1990s, RFID has steadily evolved from an experimental enhancement to a widely adopted tool for improving circulation, inventory management, and patron experience. As libraries continue to modernize and adapt to changing user expectations, understanding RFID, including its capabilities, limitations, and long-term implications, is essential for informed decision-making. This article provides a thorough overview of RFID technology in libraries, synthesizing research, case studies, and industry standards to help public librarians evaluate whether RFID is the right investment for their institutions. Understanding RFID Technology in Libraries RFID tags come in two primary forms: active and passive. Libraries exclusively use passive tags, which do not require an internal power source and are small enough to be concealed within books and media cases. Passive tags contain information that is picked up by a scanner, while active tags emit their own signals. In library settings, RFID tags store essential item information like title, author, call number, and location and can be read without direct line-of-sight. Libraries of any size are eligible to participate. Fulton County Library System youth services librarian, Grace Stannard, shows off her Laufey Book Club library card, while purchasing a new Laufey READ poster at the ALA Annual Conference in Chicago. items.title: Making the Invisible Visible: Advocacy at the Heart of Public Libraries
items.raw_text: Public libraries face no shortage of challenges today. Ongoing censorship efforts, increasing threats to staff safety, growing public distrust of institutions, and rapid technological change continue to reshape the work of libraries and the people who sustain them. In this environment, advocacy matters more than ever. That message came through clearly at the 2026 Public Library Association conference, where many sessions focused on helping librarians strengthen their advocacy skills. At the heart of every library are the workers who understand its value best and are often its strongest advocates. One session I attended, “Advocacy at the Core of ALA’s Next 150 Years,” featured Sam Helmick, Maria McCauley, Daniel Montgomery, and Lisa Varga. The panel offered practical strategies for advocacy, including using easy digital tools to contact legislators, participating in National Library Legislative Day, supporting legislation such as the Right to Read Act, and inviting elected officials into library spaces to see the work firsthand. Another standout session, “Advocacy Strategies for Getting Things Done,” featured Lisa Wells, Amanda Kordeliski, Tim Miller, Gail Oehler, and Kelly Sitzman from libraries across Oklahoma. Their discussion focused on the power of quiet advocacy. Quiet advocacy means building relationships with legislators before you urgently need their support. items.title: Creating Meaningful Connections Through Memory Cafés
items.raw_text: The 2026 Public Library Association conference featured many excellent sessions focused on programming and community engagement, but one that especially resonated with me was “Memory Cafés in Libraries: Creating Meaningful Connections,” presented by Christina M. Johnson, Allan M. Kleiman, and Susan H. McFadden. Before attending this session, I had heard of Memory Cafés but did not fully understand what they were, who they served, or how they could be integrated into library programming. By the end of the hour, I felt equipped with the knowledge and resources needed to successfully bring this type of program to my own library. The library where I work is within walking distance of two senior living apartment buildings, and our community of 16,000 is also home to several assisted living facilities. Older adults often make up the majority of attendees at our programs, so as the staff member responsible for adult programming, I attended PLA hoping to learn about meaningful services for this audience. The session began by defining the core audience for a Memory Café: people living with dementia, whether formally diagnosed or not, their caregivers, and volunteers interested in learning more. The presenters emphasized the importance of clearly communicating this audience in promotional materials. Christina M. items.title: From Skeptic to Troublemaker: One Book Club Idea That Changed My Mind
items.raw_text: I’ll admit it: library book clubs make me instantly wary. People constantly ask libraries to offer them, only to never actually show up. And a book club for kids? Forget about it. They already have plenty of assigned reading at school. So when I attended Tanvi Rastogi’s session, “Speak Up: Using Middle Grade Books to Build Allyship Muscles,” I assumed it would be a low-stakes hour to slowly wake up and drink my coffee. Friends, I didn’t even need the coffee. I left energized. Rastogi’s book club model, Good Books Young Troublemakers (GBYT), is far more than a well-intentioned idea with a catchy title. It has its own website and 501(c)(3) tax-exempt status, a sign of just how thoroughly Rastogi developed this concept after first dreaming it up in the shower. She has created a turnkey model for anyone interested in starting a chapter. Each month features a thoughtfully selected recently published title, paired with a robust downloadable discussion guide. New chapter leaders can request a starter kit complete with stickers and bookmarks mailed directly to them. Best of all, it’s free, though donations are encouraged, and there’s a pretty fun sticker if you decide to support the work. So what is GBYT all about? items.title: Renewed and Reenergized: A Rural Librarian’s PLA 2026 Experience
items.raw_text: It was a true gift to attend the recent Public Library Association Conference in Minneapolis. It had been 12 years since I last attended PLA, and I had forgotten just how exciting and energizing it can be to gather with library workers from across the country. I am still reflecting on Dr. Benjamin’s perspective on AI, which she reframed, in part, as Ancestral Intelligence rather than Artificial Intelligence. items.title: Finding Connection and Community at PLA 2026
items.raw_text: Attending the PLA 2026 Conference in Minneapolis was an enriching experience in my professional development as a second-year MLIS student. I first learned about PLA while working as a Library Assistant and later as a Library Associate at my local public library system in Maryland. Although I am not a Spanish speaker, I appreciated the Spanish live captions throughout the presentation. One of the most valuable aspects of the session was the presenters’ candid discussion of what did not work. For example, they found that holding community meetings indoors at an apartment complex limited resident participation. Their experience highlighted the importance of time, persistence, and relationship-building with community management. items.title: “I Wanted To Write Something That Felt More Like A Hug” – DeAndra Davis On Her Enchanting Coming-Of-Age Novel
items.raw_text: Despite being smart, funny, and her class’s valedictorian, Jaliya has spent much of her high school career ignored by her classmates. After graduation, her dad encourages her to leave their South Florida home to spend the summer in Jamaica with her family, who she hasn’t seen in several years. Although reluctant to do so, Jaliya changes her mind after receiving an unsigned letter postmarked from Jamaica asking when she’s going to return there. Convinced the letter is from her estranged mother, Jaliya devises a plan to return to Jamaica, find her mother, and figure out once and for all why she left their family long ago. Yet once she’s back in Jamaica, Jaliya’s life grows unexpectedly richer. She reconnects with childhood friends and finds herself caught in a love triangle between her schoolgirl crush, Andre, and an intriguing new girl, India, who has just moved to her cousin’s neighborhood. DeAndra Davis’s The Lovers, The Liars, And Me is a tender coming-of-age story that sensitively handles estrangement, coming out, cultural identity, and the complicated feelings that arise when you enter the adult world. items.title: Expanding Access Through Inclusive Collections
items.raw_text: Receiving a scholarship to attend PLA 2026 in Minneapolis gave me the opportunity to learn from innovative libraries and inspiring information professionals. One session in particular, “Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities,” presented by Plano Public Library and Libraries for All LLC, reinforced a simple but urgent idea: if members of our community cannot meaningfully use our materials, we are not fully meeting our mission. Access is about more than having a collection. It is about ensuring that everyone can engage with and benefit from it. The session highlighted how people with disabilities are often underserved by traditional library collections. While many libraries offer large print, braille, and other accessible formats, these resources do not address the full range of patron needs. Some readers may have physical disabilities that make turning pages difficult. Others may benefit from visual supports, tactile elements, or alternative ways of interacting with a text. Without intentional efforts to address these needs, some community members may remain excluded from library services. Before attending the session, my understanding of accessibility largely centered on traditional formats such as large print and braille. Learning about adaptive books expanded that perspective. items.title: Connections, Ideas, and a Little Hope: Reflections from PLA 2026
items.raw_text: I had the distinct honor of attending PLA 2026 in Minneapolis thanks to a PLA scholarship. As an eastern North Dakota native, Minneapolis is a familiar destination, but spending several days surrounded by thousands of energized library professionals made the city feel vibrant and new, despite the wind, cold, snow, and more wind. The connections, reunions, and conversations I experienced throughout the conference reminded me why gatherings like PLA matter. Alongside reconnecting with colleagues and making new professional connections, I left with fresh ideas, practical tools, and renewed optimism about the future of libraries. What impressed me most was how scalable the ideas felt. Calgary Public Library serves nearly 1,000 employees, while my library employs roughly 30 staff members, yet many of the concepts felt immediately applicable. items.title: Building More Inclusive Libraries for Patrons with Disabilities
items.raw_text: At every conference I attend, I hope to leave with at least one idea I can realistically adapt and implement at my own library. At PLA 2026, I found that inspiration in my very first session: *”Creating Inclusive Collections for Patrons with Disabilities.”* Presenter Courtney Walker, founder of Libraries for All, shared how her experience as a school librarian led her to rethink traditional picture book collections for students with disabilities. She noticed that many students were not engaging with standard picture books, often returning them unread or damaged. In some cases, families stopped checking out books altogether. Seeking a solution, Walker adapted a resource commonly used in classrooms: laminated books enhanced with sensory and interactive elements. By modifying these materials for library use and creating durable books with touch-and-feel components, she found that students with disabilities engaged more actively with stories and enjoyed more positive and equitable reading experiences. Walker now works as a consultant through Libraries for All and collaborated with fellow presenters Janet Cox and Maggie Fox of Plano Public Library (PPL) in Texas to develop a full collection of adapted books. Their team selected popular picture books, organized volunteer workshops to create adapted versions, trained staff to support the collection, and developed cataloging practices for these unique materials. items.title: Information Strategies for Libraries in the Age of AI
items.raw_text: Librarians must actively adapt to an information landscape increasingly shaped by artificial intelligence (AI), search engine optimization (SEO), and algorithm-driven content. During the PLA 2026 session, *”Trust & Verify: Information Accuracy in the Age of SEO, AI, and Algorithms,”* Nathaniel Burnard, Systems Services Manager at Allen County Public Library, offered a practical and timely examination of how these forces influence the way we, and our patrons, discover and evaluate information. As a 2026 PLA scholarship recipient, I had the opportunity to attend Burnard’s insightful presentation in Minneapolis. Burnard began by explaining the differences between misinformation, disinformation, and malinformation (MDM). While these terms are often used interchangeably, they differ based on the intent behind the creation or sharing of information. Misinformation is false or inaccurate information shared without intent to deceive. Disinformation is deliberately false information created to manipulate, mislead, or cause harm. Malinformation contains truthful information that is presented in a misleading, sensationalized, or harmful way. To help identify MDM, Burnard encouraged attendees to ask critical questions such as, “Does this content provoke a strong emotional response?” and “Does it use small pieces of valid information that have been exaggerated or distorted?” He also emphasized the importance of avoiding engagement with misleading content.
